title: India's Children Are Losing Their Eyesight to Screens — and Doctors Say the Damage Is Preventable
excerpt: AIIMS experts and the All India Ophthalmological Society sound the alarm on a childhood myopia surge driven by six-plus hours of daily screen time, issuing new guidelines that every NRI parent with children in India — or abroad — should read.
body:
A ten-year-old boy in Delhi was brought to an ophthalmologist after his parents noticed him holding books barely inches from his face. The diagnosis: progressive myopia, a condition that eye specialists say is now reaching epidemic proportions among Indian school-age children. The boy is far from alone.

Dr Namrata Sharma, Chairperson of the Scientific Committee at the All India Ophthalmological Society (AIOS) and Professor of Ophthalmology at AIIMS New Delhi, says the medical community can no longer treat this as a routine refractive error. "Environmental influences such as extended near work, excessive screen use, and limited outdoor activities are modifiable risk factors that require immediate attention," she said, calling for a shift from reactive treatment to proactive prevention.

## The Numbers Behind the Crisis

A landmark longitudinal study of 10,000 Delhi schoolchildren — the North India Myopia Study — found an annual myopia incidence of 3.4 per cent, with progression observed in nearly half of children already diagnosed. Hours of reading, computer and video-game use, and television were all significant risk factors. Outdoor activity of more than two hours daily, by contrast, was strongly protective.

Globally, myopia prevalence is projected to reach 40 per cent of the world's population by 2050, up from 23 per cent in 2016. In India specifically, a prediction model published in a peer-reviewed journal estimates myopia prevalence among urban children aged five to fifteen will rise to nearly 32 per cent by 2030. East and Southeast Asia already report myopia rates of 80 to 90 per cent among school-age children — a trajectory India could follow without intervention.

The culprit is not a single device but a constellation of modern habits. Children now average more than six hours of daily screen exposure, split between online schoolwork, educational videos, and recreational use. That sustained close-distance focus, combined with the sharp decline in outdoor play since the pandemic, creates precisely the conditions that accelerate myopia in developing eyes.

## What the New Guidelines Say

The AIOS guidelines released this month lay out a tiered approach by age. Children under two should have virtually no screen exposure. Those aged two to five should be limited to less than one hour daily under supervision. For five-to-ten-year-olds, recreational screen time should stay under two hours. For older children, where educational demands make strict caps impractical, the emphasis shifts to structured breaks.

The centrepiece is the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for at least 20 seconds. Simple as it sounds, ophthalmologists say it is one of the most effective interventions available.

Other recommendations include annual eye examinations for all school-age children, vision screenings in schools, maintaining proper reading distance (desktops and laptops are better than handheld devices), studying in well-lit rooms rather than reclining with a phone, and — critically — a minimum of two hours of outdoor activity every day. The protective factor, researchers believe, is not exercise per se but cumulative exposure to natural light.

## The Diaspora Dimension

For NRI parents, this is a global problem with a specifically Indian edge. Indian-American, British-Indian, and Canadian-Indian families often maintain close ties with relatives in India and send children for extended summer visits or schooling. The screen-time patterns that drive myopia in Indian cities are mirrored — sometimes amplified — in diaspora households where children juggle multiple devices across online tuition, social media, and streaming.

Parents who grew up without spectacles may be slow to notice the signs: squinting at distant objects, sitting too close to the television, frequent headaches, or difficulty copying from the classroom board. Any sudden change in these behaviours, doctors say, should prompt an immediate eye examination.

The good news is that interventions work. Low-dose atropine eye drops, specialised anti-myopia glasses, and certain contact lens designs have all been shown to slow progression in clinical trials. But prevention through lifestyle change remains far more effective — and far cheaper — than treatment after the fact.

## What Parents Can Do Now

The message from India's top eye-care institutions is clear: this is not inevitable. Limit recreational screen time, enforce breaks, prioritise outdoor play, and schedule annual eye check-ups. For NRI families, that means paying attention to screen habits whether children are in Mumbai, London, or New Jersey.

Myopia, once considered a minor inconvenience correctable with glasses, carries long-term risks. High myopia — above minus six diopters — significantly increases the likelihood of retinal detachment, glaucoma, and other sight-threatening complications later in life. The sooner prevention starts, the better the prognosis.

As Dr Sharma put it, the choice is between waiting for a generation of children to need corrective lenses and acting now to ensure they don't. The science says acting now wins.
